overview: Menominee communities have deep roots around Green Bay and the Menominee River. The map uses Menomini for one record and Menominee for another; these are spellings of the same people. Its broad upper Great Lakes outlines and early dates are approximate coverage, not precise borders or a founding year. Today’s Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin governs from Keshena.

periods.title: River communities and trade
periods.summary: Seasonal settlements and trading relationships connected Menominee families across the region.

periods.title: Treaties and a forest homeland
periods.summary: Land cessions greatly reduced the homeland, while communities rebuilt their lives on the Wisconsin reservation.

periods.title: Termination and organized resistance
periods.summary: Federal termination took effect in 1961; families and activists campaigned to reverse it.

periods.title: Restoration and renewed institutions
periods.summary: Restoration reopened the way for federally recognized tribal government and continuing community development.

sections.title: A worked landscape and changing alliances

items.text: A study published in 2025 documented extensive ancestral Menominee farming at Sixty Islands on the Menominee River. Drone laser mapping revealed clustered ridges beneath forest cover. The garden beds, roughly four to twelve inches high, supported crops including maize, beans and squash in a region with a challenging growing season.

Excavations in 2023 sampled three agricultural ridges at different distances from the river. Radiocarbon evidence indicates repeated rebuilding across approximately six centuries, from around 1000 to 1600. These were landscapes maintained through generations of work, not just convenient patches of naturally fertile ground.

French fur trading from the later seventeenth century encouraged smaller, mobile bands and winter trapping camps. Families exchanged furs for knives, cloth, firearms and metal cookware. Leaders increasingly needed diplomatic skills to manage relationships with traders and neighboring peoples.

After an 1848 treaty proposed removal to Minnesota, Oshkosh and other leaders resisted. Menominee people remained in Wisconsin; a temporary Wolf River reservation was followed by the permanent reservation established in 1854. Staying close to their homeland was a major political achievement.

The museum’s account describes summer villages with rectangular bark cabins and peaked roofs, while winter camps used bark-and-mat wigwams. Households moved with seasonal work and food supplies. A family’s home life therefore involved several familiar places rather than one building occupied throughout the year.

Wild rice was important enough to give the Menominee their widely used name. The museum describes Great Lakes households cooking it with vegetables, meat or maple sugar, and sometimes parching it as a treat. Birchbark containers helped store a harvest that had to last beyond its short gathering season.

The College of Menominee Nation explains clan responsibilities through its Clans Story. Bear is associated with civil administration, Crane with construction, and Moose with camp security and oversight of wild-rice harvests. In this account, belonging carried duties toward the wider community, including how an important food resource was shared.

The 2021 Harvest of the Moon curriculum connected foods with Menominee language, seasonal knowledge, recipes and artwork by Daniel Grignon. Twenty-five sets went to school Language and Culture teachers that May. Coloring pages and food lessons offered children several ways to explore the same subject with their hands, eyes and words.

Congress passed the Menominee Termination Act in 1954, and implementation followed in 1961. It removed federal recognition and services without making Menominee people disappear. The tribal timeline describes the closure of Keshena’s hospital soon afterward, showing how a change in government policy reached directly into everyday access to care.

Community resistance included a 1964 petition and the later DRUMS campaign for restoration. On December 22, 1973, the Restoration Act became law. Rebuilding government and services required further work after that victory; the act marked a decisive reversal of termination rather than an instant repair of its damage.

Menominee forestry combines timber production with responsibility for the forest’s future. In his conference paper, Menominee Tribal Enterprises leader Adrian Miller describes balancing income with ecological, spiritual and cultural obligations. Managing a sawmill and caring for a homeland belong within the same set of decisions.

Community leaders created the College of Menominee Nation’s Sustainable Development Institute in 1993. Its work brought together education, governance, commerce and natural-resource management. Research and training grew from questions the community already faced: how to make a living while keeping the land healthy for those who follow.

Lemley and Teller’s language research followed relationships between elders, adult teachers and younger learners. Some children encountered Menominee through grandparents at home; others needed school programs for that opportunity. Their interviews show why storytelling and everyday conversation matter alongside formal lessons.

An attested example in the same study is “Maec waewaenen,” translated as “Thank you very much.” The phrase appears in a participant’s response during the research. It is a recorded modern Menominee expression, preserved here in the spelling used by Lemley and Menominee educator John Teller.

ending.text: The map’s cutoffs do not mark the disappearance of the Menominee. The nation survived land loss and federal termination, regained recognition in 1973, and continues its government, family life, education and stewardship in Wisconsin.
